strengths: Directly conditioning video diffusion on tokenized 3D joint sequences is a useful alternative to rendered pose guidance. The integration of motion tokenization and motion-to-vision cross-attention is coherent and relevant to human animation.
Table 1 reports substantial improvements in FID-VID (6.98 versus 20.64) and FID (19.46 versus 30.75), alongside the best reported FVD and LPIPS.
Table 2 provides meaningful component ablations: quantization improves several metrics, and the proposed positional encoding substantially outperforms the tested alternatives.

Qualitative examples demonstrate promising transfer across realistic people, cartoons, sculptures, and pixel art. The appendix supplies architecture and training details and acknowledges limitations involving unusual anatomy, hands, and misuse.
weaknesses: The central advantage over rendered pose conditioning is not isolated experimentally. The method combines a pretrained CogVideoX backbone, approximately 7B trainable parameters, and a newly curated dataset. There is no comparison against 2D skeleton or rendered SMPL conditioning using the same backbone, data, and training budget. Consequently, the headline gains cannot be attributed confidently to direct 3D motion tokenization.

Quantitative evaluation is restricted to six TikTok sequences. Broad open-world generalization, motion fidelity, identity preservation, and physical plausibility are supported mainly by selected images, without a systematic out-of-domain benchmark, dedicated pose or identity measurements, or a human evaluation. No uncertainty estimates are given, making the modest FVD improvement over Animate Anyone 2 (140.60 versus 144.65) difficult to assess.

The interpretation of 4D RoPE exceeds what its implementation establishes. Algorithm 1 uses fixed dataset-mean joint coordinates, broadcast across frames, rather than each token's actual moving 3D position. This is a temporal encoding plus a static skeleton prior. Comparisons against temporal-plus-joint-index encoding and actual per-frame coordinates are needed to establish the value of the proposed geometry; the 'dynamic PE' baseline uses only first-frame coordinates.

Several claims overstate the evidence. Section 4.1 claims superiority across all metrics despite lower PSNR and SSIM than multiple baselines. General multi-character animation is emphasized, but Appendix B explicitly excludes independently posed multiple people. These distinctions materially narrow the demonstrated contribution.

The tokenizer analysis does not substantiate faithful or noise-free motion preservation. Reconstruction is assessed visually without quantitative joint, velocity, or acceleration errors, and decorrelated code vectors or code usage statistics do not establish denoising or generalization. The quantization ablation supports downstream utility but does not validate these stronger representation claims.

Evaluation and data reproducibility remain incomplete. Results mix rerun baselines with numbers from original papers without establishing equivalent clip sampling and metric protocols. The curated dataset lacks a precise source inventory, synthetic-content composition, and documented overlap checks with evaluation data. The supplied manuscript also does not establish licensing or consent arrangements for the web-collected material.

strengths: Directly conditioning video generation on tokenized 3D joint sequences is a meaningful design direction that avoids intermediate pose rendering. The integration of motion tokens with a pretrained video DiT is technically plausible.

Table 1 reports strong perceptual results: FID-VID improves from 20.64 to 6.98, and FID from 30.75 to 19.46. Qualitative examples show promising appearance preservation across realistic and stylized characters.
The paper includes useful quantization and positional-encoding ablations, substantial implementation details, and explicit discussion of hand-articulation and unusual-body-proportion failures.
weaknesses: The central representation claim is not isolated experimentally. The proposed system combines a approximately 7B-parameter model, CogVideoX pretraining, and a newly curated dataset, while comparisons use heterogeneous architectures and training data. A rendered-pose baseline and a simple continuous-joint conditioning baseline trained with the same backbone, data, and budget are needed to establish that motion tokenization drives the improvements.

Quantitative evaluation is limited to six TikTok sequences, with no uncertainty estimates or quantitative out-of-domain evaluation. Selected images cannot establish broad open-world robustness, temporal smoothness, identity preservation, or precise motion control. These claims need direct motion/identity measurements and broader testing. Appendix B also states that different poses for multiple people are unsupported, substantially narrowing the advertised multi-character capability.

The interpretation of 4D RoPE is overstated. Algorithm 1 uses fixed dataset-mean joint coordinates repeated across time, so its spatial component is a canonical skeleton prior rather than the actual changing 3D geometry. Its interaction with differently partitioned 3D RoPE on image queries is insufficiently justified. Comparisons with fixed joint-index encodings and matched query/key temporal encodings would help establish what the geometric construction contributes.

Evidence for faithful, noise-free motion tokenization is incomplete. Appendix D provides projected reconstruction examples and codebook statistics, but no quantitative 3D reconstruction, temporal-error, or noise-robustness measurements. Near-zero code similarities do not establish semantic independence or generalization. Removing quantization changes FVD only from 140.60 to 142.89, so the characterization of discretization as crucial needs more qualified support.

Several performance claims exceed the reported evidence. Section 4.1 claims superiority across all metrics, although other methods obtain substantially better PSNR and SSIM. The FVD improvement over the strongest reported baseline is approximately 2.8%, much smaller than the highlighted FID-VID gain. Appendix A mixes rerun results with published numbers without enough detail to establish identical sampling and metric protocols.

The training dataset is insufficiently specified for reproducibility and assessment of generalization: source composition, synthetic-data generators and proportions, and safeguards against benchmark overlap are not reported. Licensing and consent for web-collected material are also unclear. Although the paper links code and discusses misuse, these omissions remain important for evaluating a data-dependent system.

strengths: Directly conditioning video generation on tokenized 3D joint sequences is a promising approach to reducing dependence on rendered pose maps and accommodating differences between driving poses and reference characters.
Table 1 reports substantial improvements in FID-VID (6.98 versus 20.64 for the next-best method) and FID (19.46 versus 30.75), alongside competitive FVD and LPIPS.
Table 2 provides useful component evidence: removing quantization increases FID-VID from 6.98 to 9.79, and the proposed positional encoding outperforms the tested alternatives.

The qualitative examples demonstrate appealing results across realistic people, stylized characters, and unusual poses. The appendix supplies architecture and training details and acknowledges failures involving unusual anatomy and hand articulation.
weaknesses: The central advantage of motion tokens over rendered conditioning is not isolated experimentally. The system combines a pretrained CogVideoX backbone, approximately 7B trainable parameters, and a newly curated dataset, but lacks a rendered-pose baseline trained with the same backbone, data, and compute. The improvements over existing systems therefore cannot confidently be attributed to the proposed representation.

Quantitative evaluation covers only six TikTok sequences. The broader open-world claims rely on selected qualitative examples, without a systematic unseen-style or unseen-motion benchmark, direct pose-following and identity metrics, or human evaluation. No uncertainty estimates are provided; the FVD improvement over the strongest baseline is modest (140.60 versus 144.65).

The technical novelty is narrower than the framing suggests: the method combines established VQ-VAE motion encoding, cross-attention, rotary embeddings, and classifier-free guidance. Crucially, Algorithm 1 constructs spatial RoPE from dataset-average joint positions and repeats it across frames. This supplies a fixed skeletal prior, rather than encoding each token's actual time-varying 3D location. Claims of precise 4D spatial alignment need stronger justification and comparisons against simple joint-identity embeddings with temporal encoding.

The tokenizer analysis does not establish faithful preservation of 3D dynamics or robustness to pose-estimation noise. Appendix D offers projected skeleton examples and codebook statistics, but no quantitative 3D reconstruction, velocity, acceleration, or noise-sensitivity evaluation. Code diversity alone does not demonstrate denoising or physical plausibility.

Several claims exceed the evidence. Section 4.1 states superiority across all metrics, although Table 1 shows lower PSNR and SSIM than multiple baselines. General multi-person animation is also overstated: Appendix B explicitly says the model cannot support different poses for different people. These restrictions should qualify the headline claims.

Reproducibility and comparison fairness remain incomplete. The evaluation mixes reproduced results with numbers taken from other papers without fully establishing identical sampling and metric protocols. The curated training data lack an exact source inventory, synthetic-data composition, and explicit benchmark-overlap checks; licensing and consent procedures are also unspecified. Although code is linked and misuse risks are discussed, these omissions limit independent validation.

strengths: The paper presents a promising approach to character animation using tokenized differential 3D joint trajectories, avoiding rendered pose conditions. Integration into both CogVideoX and Wan demonstrates practical architectural flexibility.

Reported benchmark improvements are meaningful: the 6B model reduces TikTok FVD from 402.14 for UniAnimate-DiT to 317.21, and the 18B model reaches 276.65. Fashion results also show competitive reconstruction quality and improved distributional metrics.

Ablations on both benchmarks support the usefulness of quantization, differential coordinates, depth information, and positional encoding. The appendix provides substantial architecture, optimization, and dataset-filtering details.
Qualitative examples show compelling transfer across stylized humans, animals, and objects, with visibly better appearance preservation than several baselines.
weaknesses: The central comparison against rendered pose conditioning is not isolated experimentally. There is no baseline using rendered skeletons, depth, or meshes with the same backbone, training data, and training budget. Consequently, improvements cannot be confidently attributed to motion tokenization rather than backbone capacity, curated data, or conditioning architecture.

Claims of arbitrary-character generalization and precise 4D control exceed the evaluation. Quantitative results cover two human-animation benchmarks using image/video similarity metrics; there is no systematic non-human benchmark, motion-following metric, depth-consistency evaluation, or controlled study of reference-pose mismatch. Selected frames cannot establish temporal quality or generalization reliability.

The geometric interpretation of 4D RoPE is overstated. Motion spatial positions are fixed dataset-average joint coordinates, whereas vision positions are image-grid coordinates with zero depth. No shared coordinate calibration is established, so this is better supported as a useful positional prior than as physically aligned 4D attention. A temporal-plus-joint-index baseline and a temporal-plus-2D-spatial baseline would clarify the actual contribution.

Tokenizer claims lack direct quantitative validation. Reconstruction on unseen gymnastics is assessed through projected skeleton visualizations, without 3D reconstruction errors, velocity errors, or controlled noise tests. Quantization does not inherently guarantee noise removal, and subtracting each joint's first-frame position removes initial-pose information whose consequences for retargeting are not examined.

Evaluation reproducibility remains incomplete despite detailed training settings. Appendix A.3 imports most baseline scores from prior papers, while exact test sample counts, reference-frame selection, evaluation resolution, and overlap checks against the curated web dataset are not specified. No uncertainty estimates are given for the smaller ablation gains.

Several conclusions are stronger than their evidence: failed optimization of alternative tokenizers or projection layers does not establish their intrinsic inadequacy; switching backbone, conditioning, and trainable parameters confounds the scaling claim; and Appendix G's assertion of superiority across every Fashion metric conflicts with RealisDance-DiT's better LPIPS of 0.053 versus 0.057.

strengths: Directly conditioning video diffusion on tokenized 3D joint trajectories is a useful contribution to character animation. Differential coordinates and motion cross-attention provide a plausible alternative to rendered pose conditioning.

The reported benchmark improvements are substantial: on TikTok, the 6B model reduces FVD from UniAnimate-DiT’s 402.14 to 317.21, and the 18B model reaches 276.65. Fashion results also show improvements in distributional quality metrics.

Ablations on both benchmarks support the benefits of quantization, differential coordinates, and positional encoding. Integration with two different video backbones demonstrates practical portability.

The qualitative examples show promising appearance preservation across stylized characters, animals, and objects. The appendix provides substantial architectural and training details and acknowledges hand-control limitations.
weaknesses: The central comparison against rendered pose conditioning is not isolated experimentally. A baseline using the same backbone, training data, optimization budget, and rendered versions of the same extracted poses is missing. Consequently, the benchmark gains cannot be confidently attributed to motion tokenization rather than other system differences.

The strongest claims concern arbitrary-character generalization and precise 4D control, but quantitative evaluation covers only two human-animation benchmarks. There is no systematic non-human evaluation, human preference study, direct motion-following metric, or quantitative assessment of depth accuracy and physical plausibility. Selected visual examples support promise rather than the claimed breadth.

The geometric interpretation of 4D RoPE is overstated. Its spatial coordinates are fixed dataset-average joint positions, while image tokens use grid coordinates with zero depth; a shared calibrated coordinate system is not established. The ablations also omit temporal-plus-2D-spatial RoPE, which would directly test whether adding the depth component helps beyond ordinary spatiotemporal encoding.

Claims that the tokenizer produces noise-free, faithful motion representations lack quantitative reconstruction and controlled noise-robustness experiments. Subtracting every joint’s first-frame position also removes initial articulation information, not merely global translation; the implications for retargeting differently posed references need analysis.

Evaluation comparability and reproducibility remain uncertain. Appendix A.3 imports most baseline scores from prior papers without documenting all relevant protocol details. Test sample counts, uncertainty estimates, and training-data overlap checks are not supplied. Moreover, tables report FID-VID, whereas Appendix J defines FVD-VID using I3D features, and its LPIPS formula differs from the standard metric.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence: Fashion performance is described as best across all metrics although RealisDance-DiT has better LPIPS; failed convergence of alternative adapters does not establish their fundamental inadequacy; and the 6B-to-18B comparison changes backbone, conditioning, and trainable components simultaneously, so it does not isolate model scaling.

strengths: The paper presents a promising approach to character animation: conditioning video diffusion on tokenized 3D joint trajectories instead of rendered pose images. Combining differential motion coordinates with motion–vision attention provides a useful architectural contribution.

Reported benchmark improvements are substantial. On TikTok, the 6B model reduces FVD from UniAnimate-DiT's 402.14 to 317.21, and the 18B model reaches 276.65. Fashion results also show improvements in distributional quality metrics.

Ablations on both benchmarks support quantization, differential coordinates, depth information, and positional encoding. Implementations on CogVideoX and Wan demonstrate applicability across two diffusion backbones.

The qualitative examples show appealing appearance preservation across stylized humans, animals, and objects. The appendix provides substantial architectural, optimization, and dataset-filtering details.
weaknesses: The central advantage over rendered pose conditioning is not isolated experimentally. There is no comparison using the same backbone, training data, parameter budget, and training schedule with skeleton, depth, or mesh-image conditioning. Consequently, the headline gains cannot be confidently attributed to motion tokenization rather than stronger pretrained models or the curated dataset.

The strongest claims concern arbitrary-character generalization and precise motion control, but quantitative evaluation covers only two human-animation benchmarks. Selected images cannot establish temporal coherence or reliable motion transfer across non-human subjects. A systematic held-out evaluation with motion-following, identity-preservation, and human-preference measurements is needed.

The geometric interpretation of 4D RoPE is stronger than its construction supports. Spatial positions are dataset-average joint coordinates, while vision positions are image-grid coordinates with zero depth; no calibrated mapping between these coordinate systems is established. The ablations also omit a strong time-plus-joint-identity positional baseline, leaving unclear whether the benefit requires the proposed geometric encoding.

Several representation claims lack direct evidence. Quantization is described as producing noise-free, disentangled motion, but reconstruction is assessed visually without numerical reconstruction errors or controlled noise tests. Subtracting each joint's first-frame position also removes the initial pose, not merely global translation; behavior under mismatched reference and driving poses deserves explicit evaluation.

Evaluation reproducibility remains incomplete. Most baseline scores are imported from prior papers, while selected metrics are recomputed. Exact benchmark sample counts, preprocessing, and training-data overlap checks are not documented sufficiently. Appendix J also labels the reported FID-VID metric as FVD-VID and gives an LPIPS formula differing from the standard definition, creating uncertainty about metric implementation and comparability.

Some conclusions overstate the results: Fashion LPIPS is better for RealisDance-DiT than either proposed model, contradicting the claim of superiority across all metrics. Overall, the encouraging results place the paper near the threshold, but the missing controlled comparison and limited validation of its central generalization claims leave it below acceptance.
